purpose: Amitriptyline is mainly used to treat depression, but doctors also prescribe it for chronic pain conditions like nerve pain, migraines, and fibromyalgia. It can help you sleep better and reduce the frequency of headaches. Your doctor may prescribe it at a lower dose for pain or sleep than they would for depression.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers called serotonin and norepinephrine to help regulate your mood, sleep, and how you feel pain. Amitriptyline works by keeping more of these chemicals available in your brain for longer. Over time, this helps lift your mood, reduce pain signals, and improve your sleep.
common_side_effects: Dry mouth, drowsiness or feeling sleepy (especially at first), dizziness when standing up quickly, blurry vision, constipation, weight gain, and difficulty urinating. Many of these side effects are stronger at the start and may improve after a few weeks.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. It can cause a dangerous heart rhythm problem if taken in large doses, so never take more than prescribed. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. It may increase thoughts of suicide in children, teens, and young adults, especially in the first few weeks — contact your doctor right away if this happens. Tell your doctor if you have heart problems, glaucoma, or seizures before starting this medicine.
typical_dosing: For depression, the usual starting dose is 25 to 75 mg taken at bedtime, and it can gradually be increased to 150 mg or more per day as directed by your doctor. For pain or sleep, much lower doses (10 to 50 mg at bedtime) are often used. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribed, and be patient — it can take 2 to 4 weeks to feel the full benefit.
